basic_info.name: CureNet (also presented as 'CureNet AI')
basic_info.description: CureNet is a single-developer, hackathon-stage Indian health app that photographs handwritten prescriptions and lab reports, runs multimodal vision extraction with a local LLM (initially Gemma 4 E4B/31B via Ollama, later NVIDIA NIM Llama 3.2 90B Vision), and converts the extracted entities into FHIR R4 Document Bundles coded with SNOMED CT and LOINC, stored in an AES-256-GCM encrypted local database (ObjectBox) with keys in the platform keystore, then linked to ABHA/ABDM via a claimed M1/M2/M3 sandbox integration. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk is that it is the closest published overlap with Module C's offline + ABDM + FHIR positioning - it even names NRCeS profiles and OPConsultRecord-adjacent resources - yet the entire claim set is self-asserted on a repository with 0 stars and 0 forks, 70 commits from essentially one author, no peer-reviewed or benchmark evaluation, no production ABDM certification, and a LICENSE file that is explicitly proprietary 'All Rights Reserved' while the README still says MIT. It is best treated as a design-reference / cautionary data point about how cheap the offline-FHIR-ABDM narrative now is to claim and how hard it is to substantiate.
basic_info.organization: Labish Bardiya (individual developer; also accepts contributions from at least one other GitHub user, Rakshika1); landing/waitlist page at jeevant.com. No company, institutional backing or team is documented.
basic_info.status: research - active hackathon/university-side prototype; latest public commit 2026-06-17, release v2.0.0 on 2026-05-29; no evidence of clinical deployment or production users

technical_features.what_it_does: CureNet is a patient-facing mobile app (Flutter) plus a clinic-workstation backend (Node.js) that digitises physical medical documents and links them to India's ABDM. The user photographs or uploads a handwritten prescription, printed lab report or discharge summary; a pre-processing step (contrast binarisation/rotation) and a document classifier route the image; a multimodal vision LLM extracts patient info, medications with dosage/frequency/duration/route, lab values with units and reference ranges, vitals, diagnosis and follow-up instructions (including Indian patterns such as '1+0+1' and brand-to-generic mapping, e.g. Crocin to Paracetamol/SNOMED 387517004); a 756-line FHIR builder emits an ABDM-style Document Bundle with Composition, Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Encounter, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport and Observation resources coded with 170+ SNOMED CT and 50+ LOINC codes. Records are stored in an AES-256-GCM-encrypted local database, exposed through a biometric health locker, an emergency snapshot, QR sharing and a RAG 'ABHAy' chat assistant, and synchronised to ABDM as a HIP and queried as an HIU under consent. It does NOT elicit a conversational history and does NOT produce a narrative, physician-attested consultation summary - its output is coded document data and chat.
technical_features.architecture: Dual-model, edge-first architecture. Client: Flutter 3.11 / Dart app with 28 screens, provider state management, flutter_secure_storage/local_auth, the `fhir` R4 package on-device, speech_to_text and flutter_tts. Inference: local Ollama running Gemma 4 E4B (~3GB, intent/titles) and Gemma 4 31B Dense (~20GB, vision extraction and FHIR conversion) as primary, with cloud fallback to Groq (llama-3.1-8b / llama-3.3-70b) and later NVIDIA NIM (Llama 3.2 90B Vision); a three-tier connectivity probe (Ollama localhost:11434 -> backend localhost:3000 -> internet) with ~30s cache chooses the path. Storage: ObjectBox with AES-256-GCM (db_crypto_service.dart) plus keys in Android Keystore/iOS Keychain, and MongoDB (Mongoose) on the backend / MongoDB Atlas in the cloud build. Backend: Node.js >=18 + Express, Sharp image processing, Tesseract.js 5.x OCR fallback, Xenova Transformers embeddings, pdf2pic/Mammoth, custom fhirBuilder.js + snomedMap.js. Integrations: Ollama, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Bhashini ULCA (translation/TTS), Tavily (web search), and ABDM sandbox APIs (Gateway, ABHA V3, HIE-CM).
technical_features.inputs: Images or PDFs of physical clinical documents - handwritten prescriptions, printed laboratory reports and hospital discharge summaries - captured by camera or uploaded, plus ABHA identity credentials (Aadhaar/mobile OTP, ABHA number/address) for ABDM flows, and free-text user questions for the RAG chat. It does not consume live clinician-patient dialogue or structured historical FHIR as a primary input.
technical_features.outputs: FHIR R4 Document Bundles (JSON) containing Composition, Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Encounter, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport and Observation with SNOMED CT / LOINC codes; locally persisted encrypted clinical records; a RAG chat answer stream; a single-screen emergency snapshot (allergies, active medications, blood type, emergency contacts); QR-based ABHA/profile sharing; and, via ABDM, care-context links and consent-based data exchange. The repo also mentions CSV/summary-style outputs in adjacent DEV/Devpost write-ups but the core artifact is the FHIR bundle.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Claims FHIR R4 (not R4B), ABDM/NRCeS profiles, SNOMED CT (170+ codes) and LOINC (50+ codes), and 'full ABDM M1/M2/M3 milestone compliance' against the ABDM Sandbox (Gateway dev.abdm.gov.in, ABHA V3 abhasbx.abdm.gov.in, HIE-CM dev.abdm.gov.in/api/hiecm) with RSA-OAEP, ECDH X25519 and AES-GCM. The README says bundles are 'validated against strict rules: no empty SNOMED codes, no placeholders, no broken references, no duplicates', and the repo contains test scripts, but there is no evidence of validation against an official NRCeS FHIR IG validator, no published conformance report, and no production ABDM certification - the compliance is sandbox-level and self-asserted. It builds generic Document Bundles rather than the specific NRCeS OPConsultRecord profile MediKiosk targets. [Real-world FHIR/NRCeS IG validation and production ABDM certification: uncertain - claimed, not evidenced]
technical_features.offline_capability: Offline-first by design: local Ollama inference is the primary AI path so 'no patient data leaves the local network'; encrypted ObjectBox stores records on-device; four documented modes are Full Edge (Ollama + backend, zero cloud), Edge + Cloud (AI local, ABDM/Bhashini via cloud), Cloud Only (Groq fallback, full ABDM) and Fully Offline (serves responses from locally stored encrypted records). The honest caveat is that the 'Fully Offline' mode cannot run new OCR/summary AI without Ollama and cannot perform ABDM/HIE-CM or Bhashini actions without internet; the offline guarantee is for local AI inference and record access, not for the ABDM exchange or the cloud-backend FHIR pipeline. Sync/conflict handling for later reconnection is not documented. [Store-and-forward sync on reconnect: uncertain]
technical_features.languages_supported: English, Hindi and Bengali explicitly via the Bhashini Translation API with TTS in the README's key-differentiator table, and the v1.0.0 release/v2 write-ups claim 22 scheduled Indian languages via Bhashini ULCA. Indian document patterns such as '1+0+1' dosage notation and Hinglish/brand-name-to-generic mapping are specifically handled. Whether the extraction itself (beyond translation) is robust across Devanagari-script documents is not evidenced. [True 22-language coverage vs claimed: uncertain]
technical_features.deployment_model: Two deployment shapes: (1) a Flutter mobile app on the patient's phone (with an on-device ObjectBox vault) talking over HTTP to (2) a Node.js backend intended to run on a clinic/workstation or LAN machine (localhost:3000), with Ollama on the same machine for edge inference - and a cloud build deployed to Render (curenet.onrender.com) with MongoDB Atlas when connectivity allows. Hardware guidance is a workstation with >=32GB RAM to run gemma4:31b (~20GB), ~3GB for the E4B fallback, and the model explicitly degrades to E4B or to cloud if RAM is insufficient. The patient-side phone flow is not the same machine as the 32GB workstation, so the architecture is split across a phone and a clinic server, not a single 4GB kiosk.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: No published accuracy, precision/recall, F1, concept-recall, ROUGE/BERTScore/BLEURT or error-rate figures were located. The only quality assertions are qualitative ('successfully parses messy handwritten doctor prescriptions', 'output reliable enough for FHIR R4 compliance', 'no empty SNOMED codes, no placeholders, no broken references'), and the repo ships test scripts (benchmark_test.js, synthetic_test.js, test_ocr_pipeline.js, verify_fhir_save.js) whose results are not published. There is no evaluation against a ground-truth prescription/lab corpus. [Any accuracy number: uncertain - none published]
performance_metrics.latency: Only one concrete latency figure is published: refactoring the RAG pipeline to run intent classification, Tavily search, clinical-atom retrieval and semantic search in parallel cut response latency from roughly 12 seconds to roughly 4 seconds, and intent classification is stated as <4 seconds. No latency is published for the vision extraction or FHIR-bundle generation path, and no figures are given for the local Gemma 4 31B on specific hardware. Hardware context is a >=32GB RAM workstation recommended for the 31B model.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Documented: >=32GB RAM recommended to run gemma4:31b (~20GB) locally; Gemma 4 E4B is ~3GB and handles all tasks if the 31B is unavailable; backend needs Node.js >=18 and Ollama; Flutter >=3.11. A full edge deployment therefore needs a workstation-class machine far above MediKiosk's ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk budget, and on that budget CureNet would fall back to E4B and/or cloud. Storage is ObjectBox local plus MongoDB. This resource gap is the most direct technical contrast with MediKiosk's constraint.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Tiny: the main GitHub repository shows 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers, 0 open issues and about 70 commits by a single primary author (plus one contributor, Rakshika1); the duplicate CureNet-AI repository and a DEV/Devpost presence exist. A waitlist landing page (jeevant.com on Vercel) is described as live; no user, clinic, record or installation counts are reported anywhere. No adoption evidence of any kind.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: None. There is no peer-reviewed publication, no controlled benchmark, no clinician-judged correctness study, no inter-annotator agreement, no fairness/language breakdown and no independent audit. Quality evidence is limited to author-written DEV/Devpost narratives and self-authored repository test scripts. The ABDM 'M1/M2/M3 complete' status is an author self-assessment against the ABDM Sandbox, not an NHA-issued certificate. This makes CureNet a claim-rich, evidence-poor entry - exactly the profile Module C must avoid replicating.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: CureNet is the most direct published overlap with Module C's positioning that the team has found, and it matters on three levels. (1) Threat to novelty: it demonstrates that 'offline-first + ABDM-native + FHIR R4 + SNOMED/LOINC + edge AI + encrypted local store' is already an articulable, demoable package in the Indian ecosystem, and even names NRCeS profiles and OPConsultRecord-adjacent resources - so MediKiosk cannot claim that combination as unprecedented and must differentiate on rigor, elicitation and attestation rather than on the buzzword stack. (2) Design reference: its concrete choices are directly reusable as a pattern - Flutter + a local ObjectBox vault with AES-256-GCM and keystore-held keys, three-tier connectivity probing with caching, brand-to-generic entity resolution for Indian prescriptions, '1+0+1' dosage parsing, and a Document-Bundle resource set (Composition/Patient/Practitioner/Encounter/MedicationRequest/DiagnosticReport/Observation) that is very close to what Module C must emit. (3) Evidence cautionary tale: it shows how easy it is to declare full ABDM M1/M2/M3 compliance, 22-language support and FHIR conformance with zero validation, which sets the bar MediKiosk must clear publicly to be credible to AIIA/Ministry of Ayush evaluators.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt/adapt: (1) the encrypted-local-vault pattern (AES-256-GCM with keys in Android Keystore/iOS Keychain) as the offline data-at-rest model, adapted to the kiosk's TPM/keystore; (2) the brand-to-generic resolution layer with an explicit SNOMED CT map, plus Indian dosage-pattern parsing ('1+0+1', Hinglish) - directly useful for Module C's document digitisation; (3) the resource set and the discipline of rejecting empty codes, placeholders and broken references in the FHIR builder; (4) the connectivity-probe-and-cache idea for choosing local vs networked paths on a flaky OPD connection. Reject: (1) the cloud backend + MongoDB Atlas + Groq/NIM fallback as the FHIR pipeline - MediKiosk is offline-first with India data residency, so document-to-FHIR must complete on the kiosk, not on Render; (2) the resource profile - CureNet emits a generic Document Bundle, whereas Module C must target the NRCeS OPConsultRecord IG specifically and be validator-checked; (3) any reliance on a 31B/90B model behind an Ollama/cloud stack, which cannot fit the ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk; (4) the absence of a conversational history layer and of a physician attestation/provenance contract. Most importantly: do not copy the self-certified 'ABDM M1/M2/M3 complete' language without producing validator output and a real audit trail.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: The whole claim set is unverified by any third party: no accuracy or benchmark results, no NRCeS IG validation evidence, no production ABDM certification (only sandbox integration), no clinical or regulatory review, and no users. The repository is a solo hackathon artifact (0 stars/forks, ~70 commits, last activity mid-June 2026), so continuity and maintenance are fragile. There is a hard licensing contradiction - the LICENSE file is a proprietary 'All Rights Reserved / strict non-disclosure and non-use' notice while the README states 'MIT' - meaning any code reuse is legally unsafe and the project deliberately forbids copying. The architecture contradicts its own offline claim in places (cloud backend, MongoDB Atlas, Groq/NVIDIA fallback, Bhashini/ABDM requiring internet) and it splits patient app from clinic workstation, so it is not a single offline kiosk. It emits generic Document Bundles, not the OPConsultRecord profile Module C needs. Finally it does no history elicitation and no narrative physician-ready summary, so it solves document digitisation, not the Module C summary problem.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: CureNet overlaps MediKiosk on positioning vocabulary (offline, ABDM, FHIR R4, India, Indian languages) but not on the actual Module C contract. Object of work: CureNet digitises incoming documents on the patient's phone; MediKiosk elicits a structured history conversation plus digitised documents at a kiosk - the history-elicitation half is entirely absent from CureNet. Output contract: CureNet emits generic FHIR Document Bundles; MediKiosk must emit one bilingual, physician-ready summary against the NRCeS OPConsultRecord IG with per-field provenance and physician attestation - neither provenance nor attestation exists in CureNet. Runtime: CureNet assumes a ~32GB Ollama workstation or cloud; MediKiosk is CPU/iGPU ~4GB and offline, a genuinely harder constraint. Trust model: CureNet self-certifies ABDM/standards compliance; MediKiosk's differentiator is demonstrable conformance and reviewable evidence. So CureNet erodes the novelty of the offline-FHIR-ABDM narrative but strengthens the argument for MediKiosk's specific, attestation-gated, validate-before-claim approach - and it is a useful reminder to publish validation artifacts rather than claims.

business_info.license: Contradictory, and effectively proprietary. The repository's LICENSE file is 'Copyright (c) 2026 Labish Bardiya. All rights reserved.' under a 'Proprietary License - Strict Non-Disclosure & Non-Use' that forbids copying, cloning, modification, derivative works, distribution and any commercial, non-commercial, clinical, educational or personal use without prior written consent; the README, however, still states 'License: MIT'. The LICENSE file governs, so no permissive reuse is available. [Which license is authoritative: legally uncertain, but the LICENSE file is the stricter and later addition]
business_info.pricing: None. No pricing, paid tier or commercial terms exist; the only monetisation-adjacent artifact is a waitlist landing page at jeevant.com (Vercel + Firestore).
business_info.funding: None disclosed. Self-built hackathon/university project by an individual developer; no investors, grants, incubator or institutional funding found. [Any external funding: uncertain - none found]
business_info.commercial_status: Unpaid student/hackathon project transitioning toward an early startup attempt (waitlist, landing page, cloud deploy). Not a commercial product, not a government programme, and openly licensed for nobody.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Direct overlaps are Indian ABDM/PHR and prescription-digitisation products: Eka Care (ABDM-linked PHR and document digitisation), Doxper (prescription digitiser with ABDM integration), Practo and ABHA PHR apps, HeyDoc AI (AI medical-record analysis and ABHA records, July 2026 activity), and the NHA's own ABHA app (DigiLocker integration and Scan-and-Share). Open-source/enterprise stacks (Bahmni/OpenMRS + FHIR, Medplum, HAPI FHIR) are the standards-level alternatives. On the offline-edge-AI axis, the relevant comparison is less a named competitor than the general availability of small local vision models.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: ABDM Sandbox across three milestones - M1 (ABHA creation via Aadhaar/mobile OTP, session management, multi-method auth), M2 (HIP care-context linking, consent acknowledgement, data-flow resolution), M3 (HIU consent-based retrieval with ECDH X25519 + AES-GCM) - using the Gateway, ABHA V3 and HIE-CM API domains. Also Bhashini ULCA (translation/TTS, 22 languages), Groq and NVIDIA NIM (cloud AI fallback), Ollama (local inference), Tavily (web search), MongoDB Atlas, and Render for hosting. It is not documented as integrated with any hospital HIS/EHR vendor.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Two readings matter for MediKiosk. First, the good news: the ABDM rails (Gateway, ABHA V3, HIE-CM), the NRCeS FHIR IGs, open small vision models (Gemma-class) and Indian language APIs (Bhashini) are now readily assemblable by a single developer, which lowers the technical moat on 'offline + ABDM + FHIR' and means MediKiosk's defensibility must come from rigor, validation, the elicitation-to-summary pipeline and the clinical/attestation contract, not from the components. Second, the caution: the Indian ABDM-adjacent indie space is crowded with demos that claim full M1/M2/M3 compliance and FHIR conformance without certification, and named players (Eka Care, Doxper) are already mainstream in prescription digitisation - so an SIH prototype that looks like another uncertified ABDM FHIR demo risks being discounted; publishing validator output, provenance and an attestation workflow is the way to stand out.

market_positioning.target_users: Indian patients/citizens (especially rural and low-connectivity users and those who read only Hindi or Bengali) who need to own and carry their medical records; secondarily doctors/clinics receiving consented record access via the doctor portal, and diagnostic labs as potential data partners.
market_positioning.market_segment: Consumer PHR / medical-document digitisation and ABDM interoperability tooling - a patient-side ABHA-linked record vault with AI extraction. It touches pre-consultation document intake but does not sit in clinical-summary generation, ambient scribing, HIS, or AYUSH software.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: CureNet positions itself as "India's first ABDM-native, offline-first health intelligence platform", built "for healthcare settings where reliable internet is a luxury", so that "every Indian" gets "real ownership of their medical records" through ABDM and the DPDP Act 2023. It markets point-camera scanning of any prescription into FHIR R4, a biometric health locker, a RAG AI assistant in 22 Indian languages, an emergency snapshot and consent-based QR sharing, and explicitly argues that running models locally (open-weights Gemma 4 under Apache 2.0) means "no third-party data processor", hence privacy by architecture. It claims full ABDM M1/M2/M3 milestone compliance as a central credibility point.
